newsitem.title: USA: Smog ingredient may help babies with lung problems.
newsitem.headline: Smog ingredient may help babies with lung problems.

text.p: Nitric oxide, an ingredient in smog that is also used by the body to control blood pressure, kill tumour cells and boost erections, may help newborn babies with lung problems breathe more easily.

Two studies in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine show that newborn babies with breathing difficulties did not need drastic treatment if they inhaled small amounts of the gas. The breathing problems studied were caused by high blood pressure in the arteries that feed blood to the lungs, the inhalation of contaminated amniotic fluid, or a malformation of the diaphragm, which draws air into the lung.
The treatment does not, however, reduce the risk of death.

In the first study, led by Dr. Richard Ehrenkranz of the Yale University School of Medicine, 114 newborns on ventilators received a 20-parts-per-million mixture of nitric oxide while 121 in a control group got 100 percent oxygen.
In the control group 17 percent of the babies died. Of those who received the nitric oxide treatment, 14 percent died, which is not considered statistically different.

But the Ehrenkranz team did see a big difference when they looked at how many newborns in each group needed surgery in which blood is taken from a large vein, oxygenated and returned to the body via the neck. By that standard, 39 percent of the nitric oxide recipients needed surgery versus 54 percent of those who did not get the gas.

The surgery is expensive, causes brain problems in 20 percent of patients and destroys one of two vital arteries that send blood from the heart to the brain. Of the 1,000 newborns who undergo the surgery annually, only about 82 percent survive, according to the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD).

In the other multi-hospital study, a group led by Dr. Jesse Roberts of Massachusetts General Hospital tested nitric oxide or nitrogen on 58 full-term infants whose lack of oxygen was caused by pulmonary hypertension -- high blood pressure in the arteries sending blood to the lungs.

Nitrogen was given to the control group because it is already plentiful in normal air. Inhaling nitric oxide doubled the amount of oxygen in the body in 16 out of 30 babies. Breathing nitrogen had the same effect in only two of 28 newborns in the control group.
Nitric oxide is believed to relax blood vessels in the lung so more oxygen can be absorbed.

As in the Ehrenkranz study, the Roberts team found that fewer babies given nitric oxide needed to be hooked to the machine that directly adds oxygen to the blood. Only 40 percent of the babies getting nitric oxide needed that treatment versus 71 percent in the control group.
The Roberts team said the findings were intriguing because "current treatments are often ineffective" and hooking someone up to a machine to add oxygen to the blood could be risky.

Dr. Linda Wright of the NICHD, one of Ehrenkranz's coauthors, said that because of those risks and the costs, "a non-invasive alternative treatment such as nitric oxide therapy represents a major advance."
